html:
An oasis city on the Zarafshan River in what is now Uzbekistan, for over two thousand years a stop on the Silk Road and one of the great centres of Islamic learning in Central Asia.

It was a Sogdian trading town before the Arab conquest in the early 700s. Under the Samanids, who made it their capital in the 800s and 900s, it was a centre of Persian culture and of the new written Persian. The Samanid Mausoleum survives from those years. The scholar al-Bukhari, whose collection of the sayings of the Prophet is the most trusted in Sunni Islam, was born there, and Avicenna was born nearby and studied in its royal library.

In 1127 the Karakhanid rulers built the Kalyan Minaret. In 1220 Genghis Khan took and burned the city during the Mongol invasion of Khwarazm, though the minaret was spared.

From the 1500s Bukhara was the capital of Uzbek khanates, later the Emirate of Bukhara. It was famous for its madrasas, its bazaars and its slave market. Russia made the emirate a protectorate in 1868, and the Red Army overthrew the last emir in 1920. A Jewish community lived there for centuries; most left for Israel and the United States after 1991. The old city is a World Heritage Site.
sum: An oasis city on the Zarafshan River in what is now Uzbekistan, for over two thousand years a stop on the Silk Road and one of the great centres of Islamic learning in Central Asia.
